choices: Focal epilepsy, treated with levetiracetam
Absence epilepsy, treated with ethosuximide
Psychogenic non-epileptic events, treated with psychiatric and behavioral therapy
Status epilepticus, treated with anesthesia induction
quiz.why: The lack of an EEG correlate along with asynchronous movements, resisted eye opening, and rapid return of awareness defines psychogenic non-epileptic events, which are treated with psychological and behavioral therapy rather than antiepileptic medications.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old typist reports nighttime numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that improves with shaking the hand. Which structure is most likely compressed and where?
choices: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck
Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
quiz.why: Median nerve distribution symptoms (thumb, index, middle finger, sparing the little finger) worsening at night and relieved by shaking ('flick sign') is classic for carpal tunnel syndrome.

quiz.q: A patient develops numbness in the little finger and weakness of finger abduction after repeatedly leaning on a flexed elbow at a desk. Which nerve is compressed and at what site?
choices: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Sciatic nerve at the piriformis
quiz.why: The ulnar nerve is exposed at the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, and chronic flexion or compression there produces little finger and half ring finger numbness with intrinsic hand muscle weakness.

quiz.q: A motorcyclist sustains a mid-shaft humeral fracture and now cannot extend the wrist or fingers, with numbness over the dorsal web space between thumb and index finger. Which nerve is injured?
choices: Ulnar nerve
Radial nerve
Median nerve
Axillary nerve
quiz.why: The radial nerve wraps around the mid-shaft humerus in the spiral groove, so a humeral shaft fracture classically injures it, producing wrist drop and dorsal web space numbness.

quiz.q: A patient with a fibular head fracture develops a high-stepping gait and numbness over the top of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
choices: Tibial nerve
Sural nerve
Common peroneal nerve
Femoral nerve
quiz.why: The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, making it vulnerable to fracture there, and its injury produces foot drop with a high-stepping gait and dorsal foot numbness.

quiz.q: A patient has low back pain radiating down the posterior thigh past the knee, weak ankle plantar flexion, and an absent Achilles reflex. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
choices: L4
L5
S3
S1
quiz.why: Weak plantar flexion and an absent Achilles reflex localize to the S1 nerve root, commonly compressed by an L5-S1 disc herniation, distinct from L5 which affects toe extension and dorsiflexion.

quiz.q: An elderly patient with cervical spondylosis falls, hyperextending the neck, and develops arm weakness far worse than leg weakness with a normal cervical X-ray. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Central cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Séquard syndrome
Cauda equina syndrome
quiz.why: Central cord syndrome follows hyperextension in an older, spondylotic spine and produces disproportionate arm weakness, and it notably can occur without any fracture visible on imaging because the cord is injured by a canal already narrowed by degenerative disease.

quiz.q: After aortic surgery, a patient develops bilateral leg paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the injury level, but vibration and proprioception remain intact. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Posterior cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Séquard syndrome
Central cord syndrome
quiz.why: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) but not the posteriorly located dorsal columns, so its compromise during aortic surgery causes motor and pain/temperature loss with preserved vibration and position sense.

quiz.q: A patient with a stab wound to the right side of the spinal cord at T8 has right leg weakness and loss of vibration on the right, with loss of pain and temperature on the left starting around T10. What syndrome is this?
choices: Central cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome
Brown-Séquard syndrome
Posterior cord syndrome
quiz.why: This is Brown-Séquard syndrome, a cord hemisection: ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss beginning a level or two below the lesion, because the spinothalamic tract has already crossed.

quiz.q: A patient presents with new saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and bilateral leg weakness after several weeks of worsening low back pain. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Schedule outpatient MRI within the next week
Prescribe NSAIDs and physical therapy, reassess in a month
Perform straight leg raise testing and discharge if negative
Obtain emergent MRI and urgent surgical evaluation
quiz.why: Saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, and bilateral leg findings define a cauda equina emergency; delay risks permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction, so emergent imaging and urgent surgical evaluation are required.

quiz.q: A patient develops ascending, symmetric weakness starting in the feet two weeks after a Campylobacter gastroenteritis, with diffusely absent reflexes. What is the underlying immune mechanism?
choices: Molecular mimicry producing antibodies that cross-react with peripheral nerve gangliosides
Direct viral invasion of anterior horn cells
Autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Vitamin B12 deficiency causing demyelination
quiz.why: Guillain-Barré syndrome follows molecular mimicry, where antibodies raised against the triggering infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni) cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerve membranes, causing demyelination.

quiz.q: What CSF finding is classic for Guillain-Barré syndrome?
choices: Elevated white blood cell count with normal protein
Elevated protein with a normal white blood cell count
Low glucose with elevated white blood cell count
Xanthochromia
quiz.why: Albuminocytologic dissociation, elevated CSF protein with a normal white cell count, is the classic Guillain-Barré CSF finding, distinguishing it from an infectious process like bacterial meningitis.

quiz.q: Why are FVC and negative inspiratory force trended rather than pulse oximetry when monitoring a patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome for respiratory failure?
choices: Pulse oximeters are inaccurate in all neurologic disease
FVC is easier to measure than oxygen saturation
The primary problem is respiratory muscle weakness, and oxygen saturation remains normal until very late
Guillain-Barré always causes methemoglobinemia
quiz.why: Because the failure is a mechanical, weak respiratory pump rather than a gas exchange problem, oxygen saturation can remain normal almost until the point of respiratory arrest, so FVC and negative inspiratory force trends catch the failing pump earlier.

quiz.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine develops worsening weakness along with excessive salivation, diarrhea, and bradycardia. What is the most appropriate immediate concern?
choices: This is clearly worsening myasthenic crisis, so give an additional dose of pyridostigmine immediately
This is Guillain-Barré syndrome and IVIG should be started
This is a normal medication side effect requiring no evaluation
This may be a cholinergic crisis from excess acetylcholinesterase inhibition, so airway support takes priority over more pyridostigmine
quiz.why: The muscarinic excess pattern (salivation, diarrhea, bradycardia) suggests cholinergic crisis from too much pyridostigmine, where giving more medication would worsen the picture, so supportive airway management takes priority while the diagnosis is clarified.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental mechanism of weakness in myasthenia gravis?
choices: Autoantibodies destroying postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Demyelination of peripheral motor axons
Autoimmune destruction of anterior horn cells
Ischemic injury to the corticospinal tract
quiz.why: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, so each successive nerve impulse recruits fewer functional receptors, producing the characteristic fatigable weakness.

quiz.q: A baseball pitcher has shoulder pain, and resisted abduction with the thumb pointed down reproduces the pain. Which structure is being tested?
choices: Infraspinatus
Supraspinatus
Biceps tendon
Deltoid
quiz.why: The empty can test, resisted abduction with the thumb pointed downward, isolates and stresses the supraspinatus, the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle.

quiz.q: A soccer player has a noncontact pivoting injury with an audible pop and rapid knee swelling. The Lachman test shows increased anterior translation. Which structure is torn, and why is Lachman's preferred over the anterior drawer here?
choices: PCL; Lachman's is performed with more knee flexion
MCL; Lachman's stresses varus and valgus angulation
ACL; Lachman's is performed at less knee flexion where hamstrings cannot splint the test
Meniscus; Lachman's reproduces a mechanical click
quiz.why: This presentation is classic for an ACL tear, and Lachman's test is more sensitive than the anterior drawer because it is performed at less knee flexion, where the hamstring muscles cannot splint or resist the anterior translation.

quiz.q: A patient twists a planted knee and now has joint line pain with a click on McMurray's test. What structure is most likely injured?
choices: Anterior cruciate ligament
Posterior cruciate ligament
Patellar tendon
Meniscus
quiz.why: McMurray's test, which flexes and rotates the knee while extending it, produces a palpable or audible click when the meniscus is torn, distinguishing it from ligamentous injuries tested by drawer and stress maneuvers.

quiz.q: Per the Ottawa ankle rules, which finding alone justifies obtaining an ankle X-ray?
choices: Inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately after injury and in the emergency department
Mild swelling with full painless range of motion
A history of a previous ankle sprain
Bruising without any tenderness
quiz.why: The Ottawa ankle rules call for an X-ray when there is malleolar zone pain plus either bone tenderness at the posterior edge of either malleolus or inability to bear weight for four steps both right after injury and in the ED.

quiz.q: Why does a graded, stepwise return-to-play protocol matter for an athlete after a concussion, even once symptoms have resolved?
choices: It satisfies league eligibility paperwork only
A second head impact before full recovery risks second-impact syndrome, a rare but often fatal malignant brain swelling
Muscle strength always takes several weeks to rebuild after any head injury
Concussions always show abnormal findings on CT that must normalize first
quiz.why: Even after symptoms resolve, the brain can remain vulnerable, and a second impact during that window risks second-impact syndrome, so return follows a graded, symptom-limited protocol with at least 24 hours per stage rather than immediate clearance.

quiz.q: A tibial shaft fracture patient in a cast reports pain that worsens dramatically when the toes are passively extended, though the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable. What is the most appropriate action?
choices: Reassure the patient because a palpable pulse excludes compartment syndrome
Elevate the leg and recheck in 24 hours
Urgently evaluate for compartment syndrome, since pain with passive stretch is an early sign and pulses persist until late
Order a venous duplex to rule out deep vein thrombosis first
quiz.why: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are the earliest, most reliable signs of compartment syndrome, and distal pulses commonly remain palpable until very late because arterial pressure far exceeds capillary closing pressure, so a normal pulse does not exclude the diagnosis.

quiz.q: What is the definitive treatment for suspected compartment syndrome?
choices: Elevation and ice
Tight compressive wrapping
Observation with serial pulse checks
Emergent surgical fasciotomy
quiz.why: Compartment syndrome requires emergent surgical fasciotomy to release the pressure before irreversible muscle and nerve death occurs; waiting for pulselessness or other late signs delays treatment too long.

quiz.q: Two days after a femur fracture, a patient develops hypoxic respiratory distress, confusion, and a petechial rash across the chest and axillae. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Fat embolism syndrome
Pulmonary embolism from a lower extremity DVT
Compartment syndrome
Acute respiratory distress syndrome from aspiration
quiz.why: The classic triad of hypoxic respiratory distress, neurologic changes, and petechial rash presenting 24 to 72 hours after a long bone fracture, especially the femur, defines fat embolism syndrome, from marrow fat entering torn venous sinusoids.

quiz.q: An obese 14-year-old boy has vague knee pain, a normal knee X-ray, and holds the affected leg in external rotation with pain on internal rotation of the hip. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
choices: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, observation
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis, immediate non-weight-bearing and surgical pinning
Osteomyelitis, IV antibiotics only
Transient synovitis, NSAIDs and reassurance
quiz.why: SCFE classically presents in obese adolescent boys with referred knee pain, a normal knee X-ray, and the leg resting in obligate external rotation; immediate non-weight-bearing and surgical pinning prevent further slip and avascular necrosis.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old boy has an insidious limp and hip pain over several weeks, without obesity or a triggering injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Septic arthritis
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
Osteomyelitis
quiz.why: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head in a younger child, typically presenting with an insidious limp, distinct from the obesity and acute nature of SCFE or the fever and acute illness of septic arthritis.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old presents with hip pain, refusal to bear weight, fever of 39.1°C, ESR of 55, and WBC of 14,000. Using the Kocher criteria, what is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Outpatient follow-up with NSAIDs
Observation with repeat labs in 48 hours
Immediate discharge with reassurance of transient synovitis
Emergent joint aspiration given a high probability of septic arthritis
quiz.why: This patient meets all four Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever above 38.5°C, ESR above 40, WBC above 12,000), which together predict a probability of septic arthritis above 93%, warranting emergent aspiration rather than watchful waiting, since delay risks joint destruction within 24 to 48 hours.

quiz.q: Why does nicotine use increase the risk of fracture nonunion?
choices: It constricts the microvasculature supplying the fracture callus, impairing the reparative phase
It directly weakens bone mineral density within days
It increases inflammatory cell activity excessively
It has no proven effect on fracture healing
quiz.why: Nicotine constricts the small blood vessels feeding the developing fracture callus, reducing the blood supply needed for the reparative phase of healing and increasing the risk of nonunion, which is why smoking cessation is emphasized after fracture.

quiz.q: A patient reports headache after coughing forcefully and after sexual activity, but is otherwise neurologically normal. What should this history prompt consideration of?
choices: Reassurance without further evaluation, since exertional headaches are always benign
Possible unmasking of an underlying aneurysm or structural lesion such as a Chiari malformation
Immediate diagnosis of tension-type headache
A diagnosis of cluster headache
quiz.why: Headache triggered by exertion, cough, or sexual activity can reflect a sudden pressure transient against a weak structural point, such as an unruptured aneurysm or a Chiari malformation, and warrants further evaluation rather than automatic reassurance.

scenarios.title: Classroom case: the patient with ascending weakness
scenarios.intro: A 29-year-old man presents with two days of progressive weakness that began in his feet and is now affecting his thighs. He reports a diarrheal illness about two weeks ago that resolved on its own. He is talking normally and denies chest pain, but says his legs 'feel heavy and numb.' Walk through the reasoning a PA student should use to reach the diagnosis and anticipate the danger.

steps.prompt: On exam, strength is 3/5 in both lower extremities, 5/5 in the upper extremities, and deep tendon reflexes are absent at the knees and ankles bilaterally. Sensation is intact. What is the single most useful next question to ask?

choices.text: Ask about any recent breathing difficulty, shortness of breath, or trouble swallowing
choices.feedback: Correct focus. Ascending weakness threatening the respiratory and bulbar muscles is the immediate danger in Guillain-Barré, so screening for early respiratory or swallowing involvement changes management right now.

choices.text: Ask about family history of neurologic disease
choices.feedback: Not useful here. Guillain-Barré is typically a post-infectious autoimmune process, not a heritable one, so family history adds little to this acute evaluation.

choices.text: Ask only about pain medications the patient has tried
choices.feedback: This misses the urgent question. The priority with ascending weakness is screening for respiratory and bulbar compromise, not medication history.

steps.prompt: The patient denies shortness of breath but you notice his voice sounds slightly weaker than when he first spoke, and he coughs weakly clearing his throat. What objective measurement should be trended to guide the decision about airway management?

choices.text: Serial forced vital capacity (FVC) and negative inspiratory force
choices.feedback: Correct. Oxygen saturation is normal and will stay normal until very late, because the problem is a weakening respiratory pump, not gas exchange. FVC trends catch the failing pump before saturation drops.

choices.text: Continuous pulse oximetry alone, since it is currently reassuring at 98%
choices.feedback: This is a dangerous trap. A normal oxygen saturation in neuromuscular respiratory failure is falsely reassuring; the pump can fail well before gas exchange is affected.

choices.text: A single arterial blood gas now, with no further monitoring
choices.feedback: A one-time gas can look normal even as the patient deteriorates. Trended FVC and negative inspiratory force measurements are what actually track a progressive neuromuscular respiratory failure.

steps.prompt: Lumbar puncture is performed. What CSF finding would support the presumptive diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome?

choices.text: Elevated protein with a normal white blood cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation)
choices.feedback: Correct. This pattern reflects nerve root inflammation without an infectious CSF process, and it is the classic supportive finding in Guillain-Barré.

choices.text: Markedly elevated white blood cell count with low glucose
choices.feedback: That pattern suggests bacterial meningitis, not Guillain-Barré, and would change the working diagnosis entirely.

choices.text: Xanthochromia
choices.feedback: Xanthochromia indicates prior subarachnoid hemorrhage, an unrelated finding to this presentation.

steps.prompt: The diagnosis is confirmed as Guillain-Barré syndrome. The attending asks what treatment to start, and a classmate suggests high-dose corticosteroids since they helped a myasthenia patient last week. How should you respond?

choices.text: Explain that IVIG or plasma exchange is indicated, and that steroids are not effective in Guillain-Barré despite their role in other neuromuscular disease
choices.feedback: Correct and worth stating clearly, since this is a commonly confused point between two different neuromuscular diseases with different treatments.

choices.text: Agree that steroids should be started immediately
choices.feedback: Steroids are not effective for Guillain-Barré and should not be used; this reflects confusion between Guillain-Barré and myasthenia gravis management.

choices.text: Say no treatment is needed since the patient is not yet in respiratory failure
choices.feedback: IVIG or plasma exchange should be started once the diagnosis is confirmed, regardless of whether respiratory failure has occurred yet, to limit progression.

steps.prompt: Final teaching point before wrapping up the case. What is the single most important takeaway to emphasize to the group?

choices.text: Track FVC and negative inspiratory force, not oxygen saturation, because neuromuscular respiratory failure is a pump problem that saturation detects too late
choices.feedback: This is the core, testable lesson of the case and the point most likely to prevent a missed deterioration in practice.

choices.text: Guillain-Barré always requires ICU admission regardless of exam findings
choices.feedback: Not every case requires ICU admission; the decision is guided by trended respiratory measures and bulbar function, not a blanket rule.

choices.text: Reflexes are unaffected in Guillain-Barré, so their presence or absence is not diagnostically useful
choices.feedback: This is incorrect. Diffuse early areflexia is a key diagnostic feature of Guillain-Barré and should not be dismissed.

scenarios.debrief: Guillain-Barré syndrome is diagnosed clinically (ascending weakness, diffuse areflexia, recent infectious trigger) and supported by albuminocytologic dissociation on CSF. The single highest-yield safety point is that respiratory failure in this disease is a mechanical pump problem, so pulse oximetry stays falsely reassuring until very late; trended FVC and negative inspiratory force are what actually catch a patient before respiratory arrest. Treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange, never steroids.

scenarios.title: Classroom case: the ankle that will not bear weight
scenarios.intro: A 4-year-old girl is brought in by her parents refusing to walk and crying when her right hip is moved. They say she had a mild cold last week and now has a fever. Work through how to distinguish a benign explanation from a surgical emergency.

steps.prompt: Vitals show a temperature of 39.0°C. She refuses to bear weight on the right leg and holds the hip flexed and externally rotated. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude first, and why?

choices.text: Septic arthritis, because delayed treatment can permanently destroy the joint within 24 to 48 hours
choices.feedback: Correct. Septic arthritis is the diagnosis that cannot be missed here, since cartilage-damaging enzymes from the infection can cause irreversible joint destruction quickly if drainage is delayed.

choices.text: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, because it is the most common cause of childhood limp
choices.feedback: Perthes disease is a reasonable consideration for an atraumatic limp, but it is not the acute, fever-associated emergency that must be excluded first in this presentation.

choices.text: A simple viral illness causing generalized malaise, no further workup needed
choices.feedback: This dismisses a fever plus refusal to bear weight, which must be worked up for a joint infection before being attributed to a viral illness alone.

steps.prompt: Labs return: WBC 13,200/mcL, ESR 48 mm/hr, CRP elevated, and she is non-weight-bearing with a fever of 39.0°C. Using the Kocher criteria, how many of the four criteria are met, and what does that suggest?

choices.text: All four criteria are met (non-weight-bearing, fever above 38.5°C, ESR above 40, WBC above 12,000), suggesting a probability of septic arthritis above 93%
choices.feedback: Correct. Meeting all four Kocher criteria predicts a very high probability of septic arthritis and should prompt emergent joint aspiration rather than observation.

choices.text: Only two criteria are met, so septic arthritis is unlikely
choices.feedback: This undercounts the criteria; fever above 38.5, non-weight-bearing, ESR above 40, and WBC above 12,000 are all satisfied here.

choices.text: The Kocher criteria do not apply because the patient is too young
choices.feedback: The Kocher criteria are specifically validated for pediatric hip presentations like this one and are directly applicable here.

steps.prompt: Given the high probability of septic arthritis, what is the appropriate next step?

choices.text: Emergent joint aspiration with orthopedic consultation for possible surgical drainage
choices.feedback: Correct. A high Kocher score warrants prompt aspiration to confirm the diagnosis and guide emergent surgical washout if infection is confirmed.

choices.text: Start oral antibiotics and reassess in the clinic in 3 days
choices.feedback: Oral outpatient management is inappropriate here; the joint needs to be aspirated and likely surgically drained urgently given the high probability of septic arthritis.

choices.text: Obtain a hip ultrasound only and no aspiration unless an effusion is seen
choices.feedback: Imaging can support the workup, but with a high Kocher score the definitive next step is aspiration, not deferring based on ultrasound alone.

steps.prompt: A classmate asks how this presentation would differ if the child were instead an obese 13-year-old boy with knee pain and a normal knee X-ray. What should you tell them?

choices.text: That presentation should raise concern for slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which refers pain to the knee and requires hip imaging even with a normal knee X-ray
choices.feedback: Correct. This is a classic teaching contrast: knee pain in an obese adolescent is often referred hip pathology (SCFE), which is missed if the workup stops at the knee.

choices.text: That it would be the same diagnosis, septic arthritis, regardless of age or body habitus
choices.feedback: Age, body habitus, and the specific pain pattern change the differential substantially; an obese teenager with referred knee pain should raise concern for SCFE, not simply be treated as septic arthritis by default.

choices.text: That obesity has no bearing on pediatric orthopedic differentials
choices.feedback: Obesity is a major risk factor for slipped capital femoral epiphysis specifically and should not be dismissed as irrelevant.

steps.prompt: To close the case, what is the single most important safety principle for a febrile, non-weight-bearing child?

choices.text: Treat it as a potential septic joint until objective criteria make it unlikely, because delayed drainage causes permanent joint damage within 24 to 48 hours
choices.feedback: This is the guiding principle: the cost of missing septic arthritis is permanent joint destruction, so the threshold to aspirate should stay low in a febrile, non-weight-bearing child.

choices.text: Always start with an MRI before considering aspiration
choices.feedback: MRI can be useful but should not delay aspiration when Kocher criteria suggest a high probability of septic arthritis; time to drainage is what protects the joint.

choices.text: Reassure the family that childhood limps rarely need urgent workup
choices.feedback: This is unsafe. A febrile, non-weight-bearing child needs an urgent, structured workup to exclude septic arthritis specifically because of how quickly the joint can be permanently damaged.

scenarios.debrief: A febrile, non-weight-bearing child needs septic arthritis actively excluded, not assumed benign. The Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever above 38.5°C, ESR above 40, WBC above 12,000) stratify that risk, and a high score justifies emergent aspiration because cartilage damage from untreated infection becomes permanent within 24 to 48 hours. The contrasting case, an obese adolescent boy with knee pain, is a reminder that referred pain patterns (SCFE presenting as knee pain) can send a workup to the wrong joint entirely.
